groups.title: Technology and evolution

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best summarises the passage?

options.text: Much like evolution, technology develops slowly through gradual variation and selection, though digital technology has accelerated and transformed the process.
Even though people generally credit single inventors, technological change actually depends on networks of people and ideas that slowly combine and improve over time.
New developments in biotechnology and information technology are blurring the line between nature and machines, making it possible to design new forms of life.
From printing presses to social media, information technologies have repeatedly changed social institutions by reshaping how people communicate, think, and organize politically.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why is the success of a technology impossible to determine in advance?

options.text: Because people keep experimenting with technology by combining existing parts like chips, networks, sensors, screens, and software in new ways.
Because technologies are built in parts, so each new version can be made by improving and rearranging older ones in countless ways.
Because technology interacts in unexpected ways with nature, materials, society, and competition.
Because people's creativity and desire to make things better cannot be predicted.

questions.prompt: According to the author, technological evolution resembles biological evolution in all of the following ways EXCEPT that:

options.text: Both operate through processes of variation, selection, and replication that determine which designs persist over time.
In both cases, the success of a given variation can be determined only after it interacts with its environment.
In both domains, unsuccessful variants tend to disappear while successful ones spread and proliferate.
Both depend on mostly random changes that create new forms producing results that no one can fully foresee in advance.

questions.prompt: The passage implies all of the following about information revolutions EXCEPT that:

options.text: They change society in ways that people cannot easily predict when they first appear.
They put pressure on social institutions to change and survive, or else fall behind.
They deeply change how people think, feel, and live together in groups.
They are mainly driven by deliberate attempts to redesign politics and moral values.

groups.stimulus:
Technological change is often described as the work of heroic inventors such as Thomas Edison or Tim Berners-Lee. In reality, it emerges through an incremental process of trial and error, shaped by networks of people working in ecosystems of innovation. Technological change is an evolutionary process, much like biological evolution. Both physical and social technologies follow evolutionary dynamics and co-evolve as physical change spurs social change, which in turn spurs further physical change.

Variation in biological evolution arises from random genetic mutations and natural selection. With physical and social technologies, variation comes from human imagination and the desire to improve things. We constantly tinker with our technologies. When the smartphone was invented, it was a novel combination of existing components - computer chips, communications systems, sensors, displays and software. Likewise, the modern joint-stock company was a new combination of laws, accounting conventions, property rights and business practices. The modularity of both physical and social technologies means that each generation can build on what came before, opening up an infinite space of possible designs. Occasionally, discoveries such as fire, electricity or the laser introduce new building blocks that vastly expand this space of possibilities.

Although technological variation is intentional, it remains Darwinian. We cannot know, at the moment a new technology is created, whether it will succeed. The usefulness of a design - whether an arrowhead, a market institution or a digital platform - can be tested only through experience. Success depends on variables too numerous to be solved in advance: the environment, the available materials, complementary tools, user behaviours and competing alternatives. Designs that work spread; those that fail disappear. The same process of variation, selection and replication shapes social technologies, from legal systems to political parties.

Today, new physical technologies make it possible not only to manipulate our environments but also to alter our own biological makeup. CRISPR gene-editing tools blur the boundary between biological and technological evolution by allowing direct changes to the human germ line. Neurotechnologies can restore missing senses and augment brain function. We are even on the brink of creating life from non-living materials, designing novel living technologies. With all branches of what the philosopher Pierre Teilhard de Chardin called the “noosphere” evolving in tandem, humanity may become the first species capable of designing its own evolutionary successors, whether composed of carbon, silicon, or both.

Yet the most rapid evolutionary forces today come from information technology. Computing and the internet have dramatically enhanced our ability to communicate, coordinate and control. They underpin the explosive growth of both physical and social technologies, reshaping identities, institutions and behaviours. Language, writing, printing and digital networks are successive information revolutions, each transforming social orders in unpredictable ways. Who could have foreseen that Gutenberg’s press would catalyse the Reformation, the scientific revolution and democratic politics?

Today's Information Revolution changes our cognition, our emotional lives, our moral values and how we organise our societies. It blurs the boundaries between humans and machines and challenges our traditional modes of governance. Algorithms make decisions once left to human judgment; platforms shape our relationships, our political choices and even our sense of self. As information technologies accelerate, they exert evolutionary pressures on social institutions, forcing them to adapt - or risk becoming obsolete.

groups.title: Time and narrative

questions.prompt: According to the passage, all of the following statements reflect the author’s argument about time and narrative EXCEPT:

options.text: Though time appears real and concrete, it remains deeply unstable on examination.

questions.prompt: The phrase “simultaneity of the dissimultaneous” in the context of Mrs. Dalloway most nearly implies:

options.text: Many events being packed together into a tight timeline.
Different kinds of time being experienced at once.

questions.prompt: The author disagrees with Ricoeur’s rejection of a Bergsonian reading of Proust because:

options.text: Ricoeur overlooks the fact that Proust mainly uses figurative language to enrich his storytelling.
Ricoeur fails to recognize that Proust’s novel actually follows a clear and orderly timeline.
Ricoeur underestimates the influence of early twentieth-century industrial and technological change on Proust’s writing.

questions.prompt: “Tropes—such as metaphor, metonymy, and synecdoche—do not merely decorate narrative but make temporal experience thinkable.” Which one of the following sentences best illustrates this idea?

options.text: “Grief is a season that returns each year, no matter how carefully one shuts the door.”
“The sunset spilled gold across the river, painting the sky in extravagant colour.”
“The story begins in winter and ends in spring, marking the passage of several months.”
“Her memories were described in rich and beautiful language to heighten the emotional tone.”

groups.stimulus:
Does time exist as an objective phenomenon, or only as something humans experience and interpret? Thinkers as varied as Aristotle, Augustine, and Henri Bergson hesitated before answering this question, noting that the past no longer exists, the future has not yet arrived, and the present vanishes as soon as it appears. In response to this paradox, Paul Ricoeur proposed that time is not primarily measured by clocks but configured through narrative. In his three-volume work Time and Narrative, Ricoeur argues that narrative gives form to temporal experience, both in historiography and in fiction.

Ricoeur’s analysis of fiction focuses on three so-called “novels of time”: Mrs. Dalloway by Virginia Woolf, The Magic Mountain by Thomas Mann, and In Search of Lost Time by Marcel Proust. Although these works appear formally distinct, Ricoeur treats their temporal structures as variations of a single, largely homogeneous narrative time. This time, rooted in a Hegelian-romantic tradition, follows a logic of development, continuity, and eventual decline.

Such an approach, however, underestimates the diversity of temporal experiences these novels articulate. Rather than expressing a unified temporality, the three texts present at least three fundamentally different modes of time. Mann’s The Magic Mountain ironizes the romantic notion of historical rise and fall by staging time as both suspended and exaggerated within the isolated space of a sanatorium. Woolf’s Mrs. Dalloway constructs what may be called the “simultaneity of the dissimultaneous,’ where private memory, social routine, and historical trauma unfold at once within a single day. Proust’s novel, finally, reveals a deeply heterogeneous time grounded in memory, in which past and present collapse into one another. Ricoeur explicitly rejects a Bergsonian reading of Proust, yet this dismissal obscures what is most distinctive about Proustian temporality. Henri Bergson defended a concept of duration in which time is qualitative, uneven, and irreducible to chronology. In In Search of Lost Time, involuntary memory reveals precisely such a duration, one in which temporal boundaries dissolve. Here, time is not produced by narrative structure but disclosed through experience.

This difference points to a deeper methodological disagreement. For Ricoeur, narrative emplotment produces time; temporality is the outcome of storytelling. An alternative view holds that time is first experienced, then rendered intelligible through figurative language, and only later organized into narrative form. Tropes—such as metaphor, metonymy, and synecdoche —do not merely decorate narrative but make temporal experience thinkable. In this sense, figurative language reveals time before it is narrated.

Such an approach also invites historical context. The early twentieth century saw radical changes in how time was perceived, driven by industrialization, new technologies, and war. Thinkers and artists challenged the idea of uniform, linear time. In this setting, Woolf, Mann, and Proust do not follow a single narrative temporality but resist it, each offering a distinct response to temporal instability.

Taken together, these novels suggest that time is not singular or uniform but composed of multiple, competing temporalities—continuous, fragmented, and recursive. Rather than merely illustrating theory, they reveal aspects of temporal experience that historiography often overlooks, showing that narrative is both a literary form and a way of thinking through time.

groups.title: The precautionary principle

questions.prompt: All of the following are presented as features of the precautionary principle EXCEPT that it:

options.text: Works as a general guide for making decisions, not as a strict rule that tells policymakers what to do.
Clearly puts environmental and human health concerns ahead of economic considerations.
Applies equally to different technologies or policy choices when there is uncertainty.
Mandates adoption of restrictive measures even when proof of risks may be missing.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best explains why the precautionary principle is described as “normative”?

options.text: It replaces scientific uncertainty with legally binding rules and dictates regulatory outcomes.
It derives its authority mainly from ethical philosophy rather than from environmental or legal practice.
It incorporates value judgments about risks and priorities without justification or proof.
It reflects political preferences that conflict with the standards used in conventional risk assessment.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements, if false, would contradict the argument that “the inherently normative character of precaution renders it irrational”?

options.text: When scientific methods are used correctly, they can completely remove personal values and bias from decisions.
Moral principles are considered reasonable only when they match current economic priorities.
Even methods that are seen as objective in policy making still involve value judgments and choices about how problems are framed.
Using precaution works better than cost-benefit analysis in preventing harm from new technologies.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following policy responses would the author be most likely to criticise as a misuse of the precautionary principle?

options.text: Withdrawing an already prescribed school textbook because its long-term cultural impact is uncertain, while discouraging academic rebuttal or review.
Imposing temporary limits on the use of a new pesticide whose environmental effects remain uncertain, while comparing its risks with those of existing agricultural chemicals.
Assessing the uncertain consequences of deploying a new energy technology alongside the uncertain environmental costs of maintaining current fossil-fuel systems.
Publicly acknowledging that decisions about an uncertain genetically modified crop involve value judgments, and allowing disagreement over acceptable levels of environmental risk.

groups.stimulus:
Few issues in contemporary technology policy are as contentious as the precautionary principle. The topic features prominently in political and academic debates across multiple disciplines. Originating in the international initiatives for environmental protection in the 1970s, it first came to legal maturity in German environmental policy in the 1980s. Since then, it has been championed by environmentalists and strongly resisted by some of the industries they oppose. Its influence has extended from environmental regulation to wider policy- making, becoming a general principle of European Community law and a focus of attention in high-stakes disputes.

A widely accepted formulation of it is provided by Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration: “Where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures.’ Though called “better safe than sorry,’ this expression holds specific implications. It hinges on the presence of a potential for irreversible harm and a lack of scientific certainty. It embodies a normative presumption favoring the interests of the environment and human health rather than economic interests. It refers to the reasons for action, not to the substance of possible actions, and applies in principle symmetrically to all technological or policy alternatives.

At root, the precautionary principle involves a particular normative distillation of more than a century of experience with the unexpected consequences of new knowledges and technologies. It relates closely to principles such as “prevention”, “polluter pays”, and “clean production”. Like them, it enriches appreciations of the duties of commercial firms and the responsibilities of governments. It requires more explicit and rigorous attention to the implications of incomplete knowledge than is routinely provided in conventional risk assessment. The precautionary principle has been subject to a wide array of criticisms. One concern is that it is ill-defined. How “serious” is “serious”? What exactly does “irreversible” mean? Does “full scientific certainty” ever exist? Such concerns appear valid if precaution is treated as a comprehensive rule. However, legal scholars point out that, like principles such as proportionality and cost-effectiveness, it is not a decision rule in its own right. Rather, it serves as a general guide to the development and application of more detailed complementary methods and processes.

A further criticism is that the inherently normative character of precaution renders it irrational. This rests on the assumption that science-based procedures transcend normative content. Yet practical applications of risk assessment and cost-benefit analysis require evaluative judgments in setting levels of protection and balancing harms and benefits. Moreover, extensive literature shows that such methods involve divergent framings. When analysis is acknowledged to be framed by value judgments, the explicit normativity of precaution may be more, rather than less, rational.

A related concern focuses on the orientation of precaution in favor of the environment. Under positions prioritizing economic competitiveness, this presumption may appear unreasonable. Yet such positions do not have a monopoly on rationality. These criticisms reflect disagreement with underlying values rather than refutation of rationality. Precaution should not be invoked to suppress deliberation, argument, or dissent.

A further concern is that precaution may be used selectively to serve political or economic interests, such as protecting domestic industries or blocking technologies. Excessive reliance may also discourage innovation, highlighting the need for transparency and balanced evaluation.

groups.title: Legal insanity in Victorian Britain

groups.stimulus:
In Victorian Britain, the courtroom became an unlikely arena for some of the era’s deepest debates about the human mind. Criminal trials involving pleas of insanity did not merely determine guilt or innocence; they exposed unresolved tensions between law, medicine and morality at a moment when all three were undergoing profound transformation. In Trial by Medicine, historian Roger Smith traced how legal insanity emerged not as a purely legal doctrine, but as a contested social construct shaped by professional ambition, cultural anxieties and evolving ideas about responsibility.

The nineteenth century was marked by institutional reform and growing confidence in scientific expertise. Psychiatry, then known as alienism, sought professional legitimacy, while the legal system attempted to preserve notions of rational agency essential to criminal responsibility. These ambitions collided most visibly in trials where defendants claimed insanity. Such cases became public spectacles, reported widely in the press, and transformed courtrooms into stages where rival explanations of human behavior—medical determinism and legal voluntarism—were forced into uneasy dialogue.

At the center of this history stands the 1843 case of Daniel M’Naghten, whose attempted assassination of the British prime minister led to the formulation of the M’Naghten Rules. These rules defined legal insanity in narrowly cognitive terms, asking whether a defendant knew the nature of the act or understood that it was wrong. While enormously influential—persisting in many common-law jurisdictions for nearly two centuries—the rules also hardened the boundary between legal and medical authority. Psychiatry could describe mental disturbance, but the law reserved the final judgment on responsibility.

Smith showed that the aftermath of M’Naghten did not bring clarity but prolonged uncertainty. Medical experts disagreed sharply among themselves, divided by institutional loyalties and competing theories of mind. Prison doctors, asylum superintendents and courtroom specialists offered conflicting testimony, often blending speculation with claims to scientific rigor. These disputes reflected deeper philosophical uncertainties about free will, reason and moral culpability, as well as struggles for authority over who could legitimately speak about madness.

Crucially, Smith situated these debates within their broader social context. Class and gender shaped how insanity was perceived and adjudicated. Female defendants, particularly in cases of infanticide, were often judged through lenses of domesticity, sexuality and poverty. Other conditions—intoxication, epilepsy, sleepwalking—further blurred the line between illness and vice. In this way, insanity trials became mirrors of Victorian moral order, revealing fears about degeneration, deviance and social control.

The persistence of these tensions was made clear in the twentieth century. The acquittal of John Hinckley Jr. in 1981 reignited public outrage and renewed calls for reform, echoing patterns Smith had identified a century earlier: expert disagreement, legal acquittal and political backlash. Despite repeated reviews and criticism, the insanity defense remains tethered to nineteenth-century concepts.

Smith's work ultimately suggests that conflict between law and psychiatry is not accidental but structural. Legal standards seek clarity and stability; medical knowledge evolves and resists fixed boundaries. Trial by Medicine endures because it shows how criminal responsibility has always been negotiated at the intersection of science, culture and power—and why that negotiation remains unfinished.

The kit labelled MMM contains no Module.
The kit labelled CCC contains exactly one Sensor.
The kit labelled SCM contains no Module.

groups.stimulus: A research lab is testing six sealed kits. Each kit contains exactly three components, chosen from among Sensors, Chips and Modules. No two kits have the same composition. The six possible compositions are three Sensors, three Chips, three Modules, two Sensors and one Chip, two Chips and one Module, and one Sensor, one Chip and one Module. Accordingly, each of the six labels SSS, CCC, MMM, SSC, CCM and SCM is used on exactly one kit. However, owing to a labelling error, no kit carries the label that correctly describes its actual contents; instead, each kit carries the label meant for one of the other five kits.

groups.title: Galactic Nexus Cup

questions.prompt: What was the exact scoreline of the match between the Cygnants (C) and the Draxons (D) in that order?
How many total Orbs were scored in the entire tournament by all four teams combined?
What was the total number of points accumulated by the Boriols (B)?
How many total Orbs did the Draxons (D) score across the tournament?

groups.stimulus:
Four elite teams—the Aerons (A), Boriols (B), Cygnants (C), and Draxons (D)—competed in the annual Galactic Nexus Cup of Orb-Ball. The tournament followed a single round-robin format (every team played against every other team exactly once). A win awarded 3 points, a draw awarded 1 point, and a loss awarded 0 points. If teams are tied on points, their position is determined by "Net Orbs" (Total Orbs Scored minus Total Orbs Conceded). Data known:

1. The Aerons (A) remained undefeated and finished at the top of the points table with exactly 7 points.

2. The match between the Aerons (A) and the Cygnants (C) was a defensive masterclass that ended in a goalless draw (0-0).

3. C finished with 4 points while scoring the minimum possible number of orbs to achieve that.

4. The Boriols (B) and the Draxons (D) finished the tournament with the exact same number of points. However, the Boriols had a "Net Orbs" of exactly zero.

5. The Boriols (B) lost exactly two matches in the tournament, and both of these defeats ended with an identical scoreline of 1-2 (meaning the Boriols scored 1 Orb and conceded 2 Orbs in both games).

6. The Draxons (D) had a leaky defense, conceding a total of exactly 5 Orbs across all their matches.

7. The Aerons (A) dominated one of their matches, scoring exactly 3 Orbs and keeping a "clean sheet" (conceding 0 Orbs) in that specific match.

groups.title: Jumbled telephone extensions

questions.prompt: If Jeremy’s original extension number is 233, what is Larry’s original extension number?

options.text: Multiple answers possible

questions.prompt: If the difference between Mark and Nelson’s original extension numbers is 4, which number should be dialled to contact Jeremy after the rains?

options.text: Multiple answers possible

questions.prompt: If the difference between the extension numbers to be dialled to contact Larry and Nelson after the rains differ by 3, what is the difference between the extension numbers to be dialled to contact Jeremy and Mark after the rains?

options.text: Multiple answers possible

questions.prompt: If Nelson’s actual extension number is same as the extension number to be dialled to reach Kevin after the rains, what is the difference between Kevin’s actual extension number and the extension number to be dialled to reach Kevin after the rains?

options.text: Multiple answers possible

groups.stimulus:
Jeremy, Kevin, Larry, Mark and Nelson are 5 specialists from the Academics team of JNS Education Services. Each of them has been provided with landline phones having extension numbers 231, 232, 233, 234 and 235 (in no particular order). Due to heavy rains, the telephone lines in their section got jumbled, meaning that when someone tried to call any specialist on their original extension number, the call would go to some other specialist’s phone. The following things were discovered.

- After the rains, when anyone tried calling Jeremy, it would ring at Larry’s phone.

- The extension number that had to be called in order to reach Kevin after the rains didn’t have all dissimilar digits.

- The extension number that would ring Mark’s phone after the rains was 3 higher than his original extension number.

- The difference between Kevin and Nelson’s original extension numbers is 1.

In the third, fourth and fifth tests, the numbers become 4/5, 3/5, and 3/5 respectively of that in the first test. If we consider all the full scores achieved across all the tests, then what is the average of such scores?

If 10% of the profit was kept aside as reserve and the remaining profit was distributed among A, B and C, what was C’s share of the profit?
